etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar hatstso’n, “gate of the sheep,” so called because the flocks for sacrifice were brought in by it toward the temple.
biblical_def: The sheep gate stood at the head of the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall under Nehemiah, and it was Eliashib the high priest who rose up with his brethren the priests and built it (Neh 3:1). It is written of them that “they sanctified it, and set up the doors of it; even unto the tower of Meah they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel” (Neh 3:1). Fitly the priests began the work, and fitly they hallowed it, for by this gate the flocks were led that were appointed for the altar. At the dedication of the wall the company went round “even unto the sheep gate” (Neh 3:32; 12:39). Near it in after days lay a pool, called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, by the sheep market (Joh 5:2), where the Lord Jesus healed the impotent man on the sabbath. So the gate of the sheep points beyond itself to the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world, and to Him who said, “I am the door of the sheep” (Joh 10:7). The priests sanctified the gate of sacrifice; the great High Priest sanctified Himself, that we through Him might enter in.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem, first built and sanctified by the high priest and the priests in Nehemiah’s day.

The dictionary records it that the reader may know it for the gate of sacrifice, where the priests began and where the priests sanctified.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar hadagím, “gate of the fishes,” so called from the fish brought in by it to the markets of the city.
biblical_def: The fish gate was builded in Nehemiah’s day by the sons of Hassenaah, who “laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Neh 3:3). By it the men of Tyre and the fishers brought their fish into the city, and a market stood near at hand. It was an ancient gate, for Manasseh king of Judah, after his humbling, “built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entering in at the fish gate” (2Chr 33:14). The prophet Zephaniah heard the judgment of the LORD draw near by it: “the noise of a cry from the fish gate, and an howling from the second, and a great crashing from the hills” (Zep 1:10). At the dedication the companies passed “above the fish gate” (Neh 12:39). So the gate where men brought up their nets and their catch became a watchword both of common trade and of coming judgment; and the people of God, who pass daily in and out at such gates, are bidden to do their business in the fear of the LORD, and to remember that the same city which buys and sells shall give account to Him who judgeth righteously.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem, built by the sons of Hassenaah, named from the fish brought in by it.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar hayshanáh, “gate of the old” or “old gate,” perhaps the gate of the old city or of the ancient quarter.
biblical_def: The old gate was repaired in the rebuilding of the wall by Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah, who “laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, and the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Neh 3:6). It took its name, as the learned judge, either from the old part of the city which it served, or from some ancient and well-worn way. At the dedication of the wall the companies of them that gave thanks passed “above the old gate” (Neh 12:39), going in order from station to station with singing. The old gate sets before us a quiet but weighty truth: that the LORD’s people, in restoring His house, do not despise the old paths, but mend and set up again what their fathers knew. So the prophet cried, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). The new wall was raised upon old foundations, and the old gate was made whole; for the religion of the Bible is not the invention of novelties, but the recovery of the faith once delivered unto the saints, every man building over against his own house.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem, repaired by Jehoiada and Meshullam, named for the old quarter or the old way.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar haggaí, “gate of the valley,” so called because it opened toward the valley, likely the valley of Hinnom on the west.
biblical_def: The valley gate was that by which Nehemiah went out in the night, when he rose with a few men to view secretly the broken state of Jerusalem before he made his purpose known. “And I went out by night by the gate of the valley, even before the dragon well, and to the dung port, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and the gates thereof were consumed with fire” (Neh 2:13). Returning, he “entered by the gate of the valley, and so returned” (Neh 2:15). In the work that followed, the valley gate was repaired by Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah, who set up its doors, locks, and bars, and built a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung gate (Neh 3:13). In former days Uzziah had built towers at this gate and fortified them (2Chr 26:9). The valley gate teaches the lowly and prudent beginning of the LORD’s work: Nehemiah did not boast, but went down by night to the lowest place to measure the ruin before he built. So the wise man counteth the cost; so the humble servant goes down into the valley of the broken wall, that the LORD may be exalted in the raising of it up.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem opening toward the valley, by which Nehemiah went out by night to view the broken wall.

Nehemiah did not begin with a boast but with a night journey to the valley, that he might know the breaches before he built. He that would restore the house of God must first go down and reckon the ruin, that the work may be done in humility and in truth.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar há’ashpoth, “gate of the dung” or refuse, by which the filth of the city was carried out to the valley.
biblical_def: The dung gate, called also the dung port, was the gate by which the refuse of Jerusalem was borne out of the city to be burned in the valley below. By it Nehemiah passed in his night survey, going “to the dung port, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down” (Neh 2:13). In the rebuilding, “the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Bethhaccerem; he built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Neh 3:13-14). At the dedication, one of the companies of them that gave thanks went upon the wall toward the dung gate, compassing the city with praise (Neh 12:31). It was no shame to a ruler of the people to take the lowliest gate of the wall, the gate of refuse and filth, and to make it whole. Herein is a lesson: in the house of God there is no work too mean for a willing hand, and the gate by which the city cast out its uncleanness was builded with the same care, and dedicated with the same singing, as the gate of the sheep. So must the church count nothing common that the LORD hath given her to do.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem by which the refuse was carried out, repaired by Malchiah the ruler.

Let no servant of Christ despise the humble task, for the LORD honours the willing hand at every post of the wall.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar há’ayin, “gate of the fountain,” so named because it stood near the fountain and the king’s pool on the south of the city.
biblical_def: The gate of the fountain stood toward the south of Jerusalem, near the king’s pool and the pool of Siloah by the king’s garden. By it Nehemiah passed in his night survey: “Then I went on to the gate of the fountain, and to the king’s pool: but there was no place for the beast that was under me to pass” (Neh 2:14). In the rebuilding it was repaired by Shallun the son of Colhozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah, who “built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king’s garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David” (Neh 3:15). At the dedication the company went by it toward the water gate (Neh 12:37). The gate of the fountain, hard by the living waters of Siloah, is a sweet figure of the gospel; for Siloah, which is by interpretation, Sent, foreshadowed the Sent One of God, and the LORD Himself cried, “If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink” (Joh 7:37). The city of God is set beside the fountain, and her gate opens upon waters that fail not.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar hammáyim, “gate of the waters,” toward the east of the city, near the going down to the waters of Gihon.
biblical_def: The water gate stood toward the east of Jerusalem, and the Nethinims dwelt by it (Neh 3:26). It is most remembered for the great gathering of the people in the street before it, when, on the first day of the seventh month, Ezra the scribe brought the book of the law before the congregation. “And all the people gathered themselves together as one man into the street that was before the water gate; and they spake unto Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded to Israel” (Neh 8:1). “And he read therein before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until midday” (Neh 8:3); and the people wept and worshipped, and afterward kept the feast of tabernacles with great gladness (Neh 8:16). So the gate of the waters became the place of the reading of the word, and the wall was crowned not only with stone but with Scripture. Here is the abiding pattern of the LORD’s house: the people gathered as one man, the open book, the word read distinctly and the sense given, that the people might understand the reading. A city is not truly restored until the word of God is set up in the midst of it.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem toward the east, before which Ezra read the book of the law to the people.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar hassúsím, “gate of the horses,” near the king’s house, by the entry of the horses to the palace.
biblical_def: The horse gate lay toward the east of Jerusalem, near the house of the king, and took its name from the entrance of the horses to the royal court. In the rebuilding of the wall it was repaired by the priests, “every one over against his house” (Neh 3:28). This little phrase carries great weight: every man builded the portion of the wall that fronted his own dwelling, so that each had his charge, his post, and his answerable place in the work. The horse gate is named also in earlier history; for when wicked Athaliah was brought forth to her death, “they laid hands on her; and she went by the way by the which the horses came into the king’s house: and there was she slain” (2Chr 23:15). And Jeremiah foretold the day when the whole city, even “unto the corner of the horse gate toward the east, shall be holy unto the LORD” (Jer 31:40). So the gate where the horses came in to the palace shall be sanctified at the last. The lesson of the horse gate is the order of the building: every man at his own post, over against his own house, that the wall be joined together and the city kept.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the building: every man at his own post, over against his own dwelling, that the wall be joined together. The work of God is not done by a confused multitude but by an ordered people, each at his charge. So the LORD foretold that this very gate should be holy unto Him, never again to be plucked up.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “gate of the horses,” named for the horses’ entry to the king’s house.
roots_lines: Horse Gate — Hebrew sha’ar hassúsím, “gate of the horses.”
It lay near the king’s house, by the entry of the horses.
The priests repaired it, every one over against his house.
Athaliah was slain at the entering of it by the king’s house.
Jeremiah foretold it should be holy unto the LORD for ever.
usage: At the horse gate every man built over against his house: each saint has his own post.
The wall was joined together because the people had a mind to work in order.
The LORD will sanctify the whole city, even the gate where the horses came in.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar hammizrách, “gate of the east” or sunrising, the gate set toward the rising of the sun.
biblical_def: The east gate of Jerusalem was repaired in the rebuilding by Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, who was “the keeper of the east gate” (Neh 3:29). He that kept the gate also mended it, a faithful doorkeeper at his charge. The gate set toward the sunrising bears a deep significance in Scripture. Ezekiel saw the glory of the God of Israel come from the way of the east, and “the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east” (Eze 43:4). And the LORD commanded that this gate of the sanctuary should be shut: “This gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened, and no man shall enter in by it; because the LORD, the God of Israel, hath entered in by it, therefore it shall be shut” (Eze 44:2). The east gate, by which the glory entered and which then was sealed, is a figure of the Prince and of the holiness that follows the presence of God. So the keeper of the east gate stands as a watchman toward the dawn, looking for the coming of the LORD; for from the east the glory came, and from the east the Sun of righteousness arises with healing in His wings.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem toward the sunrising, repaired by Shemaiah its keeper.
webster_full: EAST GATE, a gate of the wall of Jerusalem set toward the rising of the sun.
The name signifies the gate of the east, after the Hebrew tongue.
It was repaired by Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of it.
Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD enter by the east gate of the sanctuary.
That gate was commanded to be shut, because the LORD had entered in by it.
scriptures: Neh 3:29
After them repaired Zadok the son of Immer over against his house. After him repaired also Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate.
Eze 43:4
And the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east.
Eze 44:2
Then said the LORD unto me; This gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened, and no man shall enter in by it; because the LORD, the God of Israel, hath entered in by it, therefore it shall be shut.
Eze 43:1
Afterward he brought me to the gate, even the gate that looketh toward the east:
corruption_summary: A gate of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the glory of the LORD that entered by the east and the watchman who keeps his charge.
corruption_paragraphs: The east gate is a real gate of the wall, set toward the sunrising, and no movement of the present age has busied itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark Shemaiah, the keeper of the east gate, repairing the very gate he was set to keep.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the watchfulness of the faithful doorkeeper and the glory of the LORD that comes from the east. Ezekiel saw the glory enter by the east gate, and that gate was sealed because the LORD had passed through it. So the church watches toward the dawn, for from the east the Sun of righteousness arises, and the keeper of the gate must be found faithful at his post.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “gate of the east,” named for its prospect toward the sunrising.
roots_lines: East Gate — Hebrew sha’ar hammizrách, “gate of the east” or sunrising.
It was set toward the rising of the sun.
Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, its keeper, repaired it.
Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD enter the sanctuary by the east gate.
That sanctuary gate was shut, for the LORD had entered in by it.
usage: Shemaiah kept and mended the east gate: the faithful doorkeeper guards his own charge.
The glory of the LORD came from the east; the church watches toward the dawn.
The east gate was shut after the LORD passed through: His presence sanctifies the way.

etymology: From the Hebrew sha’ar ’ephráyim, “gate of Ephraim,” the gate on the north that opened toward the territory of Ephraim.
biblical_def: The gate of Ephraim stood on the north of Jerusalem, opening toward the country of the tribe of Ephraim. In the days of the restoration, when the people had heard the law read before the water gate and found it written that they should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month, they went forth and gathered branches and made themselves booths, “and in the street of the gate of Ephraim” (Neh 8:16). So the gate of Ephraim was decked with the booths of the feast of tabernacles, a place of holy gladness and remembrance of the LORD’s leading in the wilderness. At the dedication the companies passed “from above the gate of Ephraim” (Neh 12:39). In earlier days this gate had seen a sadder hour, when Jehoash king of Israel brake down the wall of Jerusalem “from the gate of Ephraim unto the corner gate, four hundred cubits” (2Ki 14:13); yet what the sword had broken, the obedience of a restored people now adorned with booths of rejoicing. The gate of Ephraim teaches that the city once breached is made glad again when her people return to the word and keep the feasts of the LORD with joy.
webster_summary: A gate of Jerusalem on the north, where booths were set for the feast of tabernacles.
webster_full: GATE OF EPHRAIM, a gate of the wall of Jerusalem on the north, toward the tribe of Ephraim.
The name signifies the gate of Ephraim, after the Hebrew tongue.
Booths were set in its street for the feast of tabernacles.
Jehoash had aforetime broken the wall from it unto the corner gate.
It witnesses to the gladness of a restored people keeping the feasts of the LORD.
scriptures: Neh 8:16

So the people went forth, and brought them, and made themselves booths, every one upon the roof of his house, and in their courts, and in the courts of the house of God, and in the street of the water gate, and in the street of the gate of Ephraim.

And from above the gate of Ephraim, and above the old gate, and above the fish gate, and the tower of Hananeel, and the tower of Meah, even unto the sheep gate: and they stood still in the prison gate.

And Jehoash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash the son of Ahaziah, at Bethshemesh, and came to Jerusalem, and brake down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim unto the corner gate, four hundred cubits.
Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: A gate of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the gladness of a restored people keeping the feasts of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The gate of Ephraim is a real gate of the wall, on the north of the city, and no movement of the present age has set itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader may see the booths of the feast set in its street and the thanksgiving companies pass above it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the joy of a restored people who return to the word and keep the feasts of the LORD. Where Jehoash had once broken the wall, the obedient people now set booths of rejoicing. The city once breached is made glad when her sons return to the Scripture and rejoice before God with holy gladness.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “gate of Ephraim,” named for its opening toward the tribe of Ephraim.
roots_lines: Gate of Ephraim — Hebrew sha’ar ’ephráyim, “gate of Ephraim.”
It stood on the north, toward the territory of Ephraim.
Booths were set in its street for the feast of tabernacles.
Jehoash had broken the wall from it unto the corner gate.
The thanksgiving companies passed above it at the dedication.
usage: Booths of joy were set by the gate of Ephraim: a restored people keeps the feasts with gladness.
Where the wall was once broken, obedience now sets up rejoicing.
Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem, the city made glad in God.
